title: Control charts
subtitle: A factory cannot inspect every item, but it can watch the average and notice the moment the process drifts.

sections.title: Two kinds of variation
sections.body:
No two bottles from a filling machine contain exactly the same amount. Every process varies, and the skill is knowing which variation to worry about. Common-cause variation is the steady random noise of a healthy process. Special-cause variation comes from something specific, such as a worn tool or a new supplier.

Statistical quality control (SQC) separates the two so we act only on real changes. A sudden jump after changing supplier is a special cause, and you should go and look for it.

questions.prompt: A sudden jump after changing supplier is…

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: A step change is not noise.

keynotes: Common-cause variation is the steady random noise of a healthy process.
Special-cause variation comes from something specific, such as a worn tool or a new supplier.
Statistical quality control separates the two so we act only on real changes.

sections.title: The X̄ chart
sections.body:
Here is the big idea of quality control: you cannot inspect everything, so you take a small sample every so often and watch its average. Plot each sample mean. The centre line is the grand mean X̿. The control limits sit three standard errors away: UCL, LCL = X̿ ± 3σ/√n (or X̿ ± A₂R̄ from tabulated constants).

Why three? Because P(|Z| ≤ 3) = 0.9973, so a healthy process almost never crosses the limits by chance: about 1 false alarm in 370. Try it: grand mean 50, σ = 4, n = 4. SE = 4/√4 = 2, so the limits are 50 ± 3·2, that is LCL = 44 and UCL = 56. The figure shows the monitoring loop an operator runs. Control limits are placed at three standard errors from the centre line.

choices.text: Three standard errors from the centre line.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Specs are customer requirements, not process behaviour.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — monitoring loop
figures.script:
diagram("Process -> Sample n items : every hour
Sample n items -> Plot mean : compute x̄
Plot mean -> Inside limits? : compare to LCL, UCL
Inside limits? -> Continue : yes
Inside limits? -> Investigate cause : no");

problems.prompt: Process mean 100, σ = 6, samples of n = 9. Find the X̄ chart limits.

keynotes: Take small samples regularly and plot each sample mean around the centre line X̿.
Control limits are X̿ ± 3σ/√n; because P(|Z| ≤ 3) = 0.9973, a healthy process gives about 1 false alarm in 370.
For grand mean 50, σ = 4 and n = 4 the standard error is 2, giving LCL = 44 and UCL = 56.

sections.title: Signals beyond one point
sections.body: One point outside the limits is a clear signal. But a process can drift quietly without ever crossing the line, so we also look for patterns: 7 points in a row on one side of the centre line, 6 steadily rising, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ. Each pattern is unlikely under pure noise, so it flags a shift earlier than waiting for the limit. Eight consecutive points above the centre line suggest the process mean has shifted upward.

questions.prompt: Eight consecutive points above the centre line suggest…

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It is very unlikely by chance.

keynotes: A single point outside the limits is one signal.
Other signals are 7 points in a row on one side of the centre line, 6 steadily rising, or 2 of 3 beyond 2σ.
Each pattern is unlikely under pure noise, so it flags a shift earlier.

sections.title: Charts for attributes
sections.body:
What if you count defects, not measure things? Then there are attribute charts. For defective fractions use the p-chart: centre p̄, limits p̄ ± 3√(p̄(1 − p̄)/n). For defects per unit use the c-chart: c̄ ± 3√c̄ (Poisson). Lower limits below zero are set to zero.

Work one: p̄ = 0.04, n = 100, so √(0.04·0.96/100) = 0.0196. UCL = 0.04 + 0.0588 = 0.0988; the LCL is negative, so use 0. A c-chart monitors the number of defects per unit.
keynotes: The p-chart for defective fractions has centre p̄ and limits p̄ ± 3√(p̄(1 − p̄)/n).
The c-chart for defects per unit has limits c̄ ± 3√c̄ (Poisson); lower limits below zero are set to zero.
For p̄ = 0.04 and n = 100, UCL = 0.0988 and the LCL is set to 0.

sections.title: Process capability
sections.body:
Being under control is not the same as being good enough. Control asks “is it stable?”; capability asks “does it meet the spec?”. Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ. Cp ≥ 1.33 is comfortable; Cp = 1 leaves 0.27 % out of spec. And Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/3σ also penalises an off-centre mean.

Try it: spec 40–60, σ = 2.5, so 6σ = 15 and Cp = 20/15 = 1.33 if the mean is centred. A Cp of 1.33 means the spec width is 1.33 times the process spread, with room to spare.

worked.why: So Cp = 1.33 if the mean is centred.

questions.prompt: Cp = 1.33 means the spec width is…

keynotes: Control asks whether the process is stable; capability asks whether it meets the spec.
Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ; Cp ≥ 1.33 is comfortable and Cp = 1 leaves 0.27 % out of spec; Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/3σ also penalises an off-centre mean.
For spec 40–60 and σ = 2.5, Cp = 20/15 = 1.33 if the mean is centred.

sections.title: Acceptance sampling
sections.body:
When a lorry of components arrives, do you test every one? No, you sample. A single-sampling plan (n, c) inspects n items from a lot and accepts if at most c are defective. The operating-characteristic curve plots P(accept) against the lot defect rate, computed with the binomial (or Poisson). Two risks pull against each other: producer’s risk α rejects a good lot, and consumer’s risk β accepts a bad one.

Compare plans n = 50 with c = 0 and with c = 2. The plan with c = 2 accepts more lots, because it tolerates a couple of defects.

questions.prompt: Plan n = 50, c = 0 versus c = 2. Which accepts more lots?

keynotes: A single-sampling plan (n, c) inspects n items from a lot and accepts if at most c are defective.
The operating-characteristic curve plots P(accept) against the lot defect rate, using the binomial or Poisson.
Producer’s risk α rejects a good lot and consumer’s risk β accepts a bad one.
